> The resulting archetypes-steadfast cooperators, conditional cooperators, game switchers, and persistent defectors-provide an intuitive map of heterogeneity in the participant pool (SI Section 8 and Fig. S10).

> Participants were recruited through Prolific using a nonprobability, opt-in sample.

> The experiment was conducted online during September and October 2024, the experimental app was developed using oTree (33), and participants were recruited through the Prolific platform (34).

> Participants provided informed consent before participation.

> All participants had a Prolific approval rate of at least 98%.

> Approved Prolific submissions took a median of 30.6 minutes.

> We linked oTree behavioral data to Prolific demographic and payment records by participant ID, removed direct identifiers before analysis, and retained valid online groups with complete scheduled 25-round records.

> Demographic information from Prolific was available for all 430 analyzed participants.

> Participants were 18-79 years old (mean = 30.78, SD = 9.94), and 223 were female and 207 were male.

> Prolific demographics, SVO categories, and condition balance are reported in SI Section 1, Table S2.

> After the game, participants completed self-assessment items, the 15-item SVO slider measure (35), and survey items measuring conformity (36) and horizontal/vertical individualismcollectivism (37).

> B: In two-stage rounds, participants were paired, saw the current opponent's previous-round PD and SD choices before choosing a PD strategy, then saw those previous cues plus the same-round PD outcome before choosing an SD strategy with the same opponent.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Cooperation across social settings requires deciding whether to reciprocate a partner's helpful behavior or exploit it when incentives change.

We examined this tension in an online experiment with 430 participants playing a Prisoner's Dilemma (PD), either alone or followed by a Snowdrift game (SD), where defection pays more against a sufficiently likely cooperator.
We also placed programmed bots-computer-controlled players following a fixed rule-in some groups.
By programming them to cooperate in PD and reciprocate their partner's PD action in SD, we created a consistent source of cooperation and reciprocity.
This allowed us to ask whether humans also cooperated more with one another.
Humans cooperated more in SD after their partner cooperated in PD, even when observed partner behavior made defection the better immediate material response.
This pattern is consistent with reciprocity, although choices do not identify beliefs or motives.
Human-human cooperation was higher in groups containing bots; coupling alone produced no detected increase in mean PD cooperation.
Separate experiments with GPT language-model agents asked whether frequent cooperation was accompanied by similar responses across games.
Despite high PD cooperation, partner PD cooperation predicted less GPT cooperation in SD in the primary pooled analysis.
This association varied across configurations and did not generally indicate payoff-maximizing choices.
Simulations using fitted human response rules illustrated the possible effects of alternative bot policies.
These findings reveal responses to cooperative partners across contexts that overall cooperation rates can obscure.
Like the individuals who participate in them, social interactions do not exist in isolation, and encounters vary in strategic form.
Business partners may cooperate in both commercial and civic settings, teammates may coordinate across distinct tasks, and neighbors may work together on separate public goods.
In each case, one potentially cooperative encounter exists alongside another, but the balance among cooperation, coordination, and free-riding can differ.
This ecology-of-games perspective motivates models of interacting, rather than isolated, games in which behavior in one setting can alter cooperation in another (1) (2) (3).

text.text: Related work on multiple one-shot exchanges shows how simple partnerdirected heuristics can support cooperation (14).

text.text: Coupled dilemmas ask what happens when information travels between settings with different strategic logics.
Consider two familiar cases.
In a shared project or costly agreement, mutual cooperation is best for the group, yet each person can gain by letting others bear the cost.
This is the logic of a Prisoner's Dilemma (PD).
In a task that must be completed, such as clearing a blocked path or handling an urgent problem, someone has to contribute.
Once another person is already doing so, withholding effort can reflect anti-coordination as well as selfishness.
In a Snowdrift game (SD), unilateral cooperation can prevent the worst outcome, while defection can exploit another's contribution (15) (16) (17) (18) (19).

text.text: Experiments also show that behavior can spill across games.
An efficient coordination-game precedent can increase later PD cooperation when action labels remain descriptively similar (4).
text.formatted: An efficient coordination-game precedent can increase later PD cooperation when action labels remain descriptively similar <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: People can carry heuristics across simultaneous games played with different opponents (5).
text.formatted: People can carry heuristics across simultaneous games played with different opponents <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: Concurrent donation games can raise or reduce cooperation depending on partner structure (6).

text.text: Closest theoretically, Salahshour (3) models a PD followed by a different game, including SD, with second-game behavior conditional on the first action.
The present experiment tests the stage-resolved PD-to-SD sign in human behavior and compares that cue use with GPT agents.
How social information carries across these contrasting settings is increasingly consequential as artificial agents enter social systems (20).
text.formatted: How social information carries across these contrasting settings is increasingly consequential as artificial agents enter social systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20)</ref>.

text.text: Bots and language-model agents can serve as teammates (21), simulated participants (22), or strategic partners (23), changing what people observe and how cooperative the local environment appears (24, 25).
text.formatted: Bots and language-model agents can serve as teammates <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21)</ref>, simulated participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref>, or strategic partners <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23)</ref>, changing what people observe and how cooperative the local environment appears <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25)</ref>.

text.text: For language-model agents, apparent continuity across encounters depends on the interaction history supplied in context, making the transfer of information between distinct tasks especially salient.

Experimental work further shows that model behavior can change when trust-game choices carry actual rather than hypothetical incentives (26), and that tested early language models can produce context-sensitive completions resembling altruistic behavior (27).
text.formatted: Experimental work further shows that model behavior can change when trust-game choices carry actual rather than hypothetical incentives <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26)</ref>, and that tested early language models can produce context-sensitive completions resembling altruistic behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27)</ref>.

text.text: These findings motivate studying artificial agents in coupled social settings, while also cautioning that high aggregate cooperation does not establish human-like use of cross-context information (28, 29).
text.formatted: These findings motivate studying artificial agents in coupled social settings, while also cautioning that high aggregate cooperation does not establish human-like use of cross-context information <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29)</ref>.

text.text: In such coupled dilemmas, two contrasting possibilities follow.
Under a narrow payoffmaximizing account, behavior in one setting is useful mainly as evidence about what a partner is likely to do in another.
The actor should then choose the best material response, even when this means exploiting a partner who appears likely to cooperate.
For example, after directly seeing a colleague stay late to keep a shared project on track, a separate urgent task may arise that either person can handle.
A narrowly strategic focal person might expect the same colleague to step in again and therefore withhold effort.
Such a rule can be locally advantageous, but it gives cross-context information a trust-limiting role.
Under a reciprocal or norm-based account, by contrast, observed cooperation is not only a forecast of future action.
It can create social credit, while defection can invite punishment, so behavior in one context becomes a basis for rewarding or withholding cooperation in another.

In the same workplace example, the focal person could instead treat the colleague's earlier willingness to help as a reason to share the later burden, even when letting the colleague handle it would bring a personal benefit.
Cross-context information can then support moralized reciprocity rather than only strategic best response.
This possibility fits broader models in which agents act on perceived or socially transformed payoffs rather than objective material payoffs alone (30, 31).
text.formatted: This possibility fits broader models in which agents act on perceived or socially transformed payoffs rather than objective material payoffs alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31)</ref>.

text.text: Distinguishing these alternatives requires a setting in which the same cooperative cue points toward opposing social and material responses.
We examine these alternatives in a controlled online experiment involving humans and parallel GPT-agent simulations.
Human participants played either a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma alone, a coupled Prisoner's Dilemma and Snowdrift game, or the same coupled game in mixed groups with cooperative bots.
The programmed bots followed a simple cooperative rule, allowing us to test whether their stable behavior was associated with cooperation among humans elsewhere in the group.
The GPT simulations served a different purpose.
Unlike the fixed-rule bots, GPT agents made prompted choices, allowing us to ask whether high aggregate cooperation also produced the human direction of cross-game cue use.
The central question is whether behavior in one dilemma transfers into another as positive social information, as a material cue for best response, or not at all.

The results show that humans display positive cross-game transfer, cooperative bots are associated with elevated human-human cooperation under the specific bot rule, and the pooled tested GPT configurations, despite high aggregate cooperation in the Prisoner's Dilemma, show an opposite PD-to-SD association that varies across configurations.
We use two standard social dilemmas.
In the Prisoner's Dilemma (PD), mutual cooperation is best for the pair, but each player can gain by defecting against a cooperator.
In the Snowdrift game (SD), unilateral cooperation still produces a positive outcome for both players, but a player can gain by defecting when the other player cooperates.
We denote cooperation by C and defection by D. The entries below give the payoff to the focal player first and the partner second:
The coupled design, in which a pair plays a PD followed by an SD, turns a familiar question into a sharper test.
Suppose a partner cooperates in the PD stage and the focal player then chooses its strategy in the SD stage.
Under a narrow material best-response account, the partner's PD cooperation is useful because it helps predict what the partner is likely to do next.
If it raises the expectation that the partner will cooperate in SD, then exploiting that likely cooperator can be materially attractive.
Under a reputational or norm-based account, the same cooperative PD action can instead function as positive social information.
The partner's earlier cooperation may give the focal player a reason to cooperate in SD, for example because the focal player treats the partner as having earned cooperative treatment.
The Snowdrift game makes these two interpretations point in opposite directions.
With our SD payoffs, the material advantage of cooperating is 1 -3q, where q is the expected probability that the partner will cooperate.
Cooperation is materially attractive only when q < 1/3.
text.formatted: Cooperation is materially attractive only when q < 1/3.

text.text: Above that threshold, an expected cooperator is materially exploitable.
Thus, if a partner's PD cooperation only raises the expectation that the partner will cooperate again in SD, best response predicts less SD cooperation.
If the focal player treats the same PD action as positive social information, reputational transfer predicts more SD cooperation.
The Reputational Coupling Model, introduced in Methods, makes this logic explicit without claiming that we observe private beliefs.

A partner's action may change the focal player's strategic expectation q, the perceived probability that the partner will cooperate, and may also carry positive or negative social information across games, summarized by a transfer cue r.
These channels are not separately identified from choices in this design.
The model is therefore a diagnostic framework for sign predictions, not a structural decomposition of beliefs and social valuation.
We test this contrast with the PD-to-SD transfer coefficient, β P D→SD .

The transfer coefficient β P D→SD measures the fitted change in the focal player's SD cooperation when the partner cooperated rather than defected in the same-round PD, holding fixed the previous-round PD and SD cues that were already visible before the SD choice.
A positive value has the sign predicted by positive reciprocity.
A zero value indicates no detectable transfer.
A negative value means that a cooperative PD cue predicts less SD cooperation.
It aligns with strategic anti-coordination only when the cue raises expected partner-SD cooperation and choices respond to the resulting material incentive.
Behavior alone does not establish those conditions or uniquely identify the underlying mechanism.
We arrange the four observed transfer coefficients, β x→y , into a transfer matrix, B: PD-to-PD, SD-to-PD, PD-to-SD, and SD-to-SD.
Methods provides the full notation, the logit/sigmoid formulation, and the derivation linking the conceptual model to the fitted transfer coefficients, β x→y.

We also use behavioral simulation models, specified in Methods, to ask whether the estimated cue effects can reproduce the observed dynamics and compare alternative artificial-partner rules in counterfactual experiments.
The Dynamic Logistic Transfer Simulation Model fits the observed transfer coefficients directly and uses them to generate predicted choice trajectories and simulated bot-policy comparisons.
The Anchored Latent-State Transfer Simulation Model is a two-stage simulation model.

It first assigns PD choices from visible prior cues, then approximates the expected partner-SD cooperation probability, q, and tests whether the residual partner-PD cue still has the sign predicted by reputational transfer.
These simulations strengthen the behavioral test, but they still do not separately identify private expectations, reputational credit, or psychological parameters.

text.text: In the PD-only control (PD-only; 26 groups, 156 humans), six participants played 25 rounds of a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma.
In the two-stage conditions, each round contained a PD stage followed by a Snowdrift stage with the same opponent.
One two-stage condition used six humans (all-human PD+SD; 25 groups, 150 humans).
The mixed condition used four humans and two bots (mixed human-bot PD+SD; 31 groups, 124 humans plus two programmed bots per intended group).
Before each PD choice in the two-stage conditions, participants saw the current opponent's previous-round choices in both games.
Before each SD choice, those previous-round cues remained visible and participants additionally saw the same-round PD outcome with that opponent, including both PD choices and payoffs.
Participants played with the same opponent in both stages of a given round, but pairings were reshuffled across rounds.
Because of this reshuffling, the design measures responses to visible behavioral cues about the current opponent rather than stable long-run partner reputation.

Fig.1.
Experimental design and diagnostic logic of coupled dilemmas.
PD denotes the Prisoner's Dilemma and SD denotes the Snowdrift game.
A: We ran three conditions: a PD-only control, an all-human PD+SD condition, and a mixed human-bot PD+SD condition.

B: In two-stage rounds, participants were paired, saw the current opponent's previous-round PD and SD choices before choosing a PD strategy, then saw those previous cues plus the same-round PD outcome before choosing an SD strategy with the same opponent.
Pairings were reshuffled before the next round.

C: Observed cues can shift cooperation through strategic expectations and through reputational transfer, but the empirical test relies on fitted sign patterns rather than direct measurement of beliefs.
D: Cooperation in the Snowdrift game has material advantage 1 -3q, where q is the expected partner-SD cooperation probability, and therefore becomes materially disadvantageous when q > 1/3.

Fig 2.
Human cooperation dynamics, GPT overlay, and observed human-only bot decomposition.
A-C: Panels A, B, and C show, respectively, the PD-only control, the all-human/all-GPT PD+SD condition, and the mixed human-bot/GPT-droid PD+SD condition.
Human trajectories are solid, GPT-agent trajectories are dashed, orange denotes PD, and teal denotes SD.
Pointwise error bars are omitted from A-C for visibility.
The dashed GPT trajectories are pooled means across GPT model families and temperatures, with model-specific trajectories shown in SI Section 9, Fig S11.
D: Human group-level means are shown with pooled GPT simulation-session means as open diamonds.
Error bars show bootstrap intervals over groups or GPT simulation sessions.
E: Human choices are separated into human-human and human-bot interaction categories.
F: Primary and covariate-adjusted logistic coefficients are shown for mixed-condition human-human cooperation.
Group-mean probability contrasts are reported separately in SI Section 6, TableS17.
Human-bot and GPT-droid observations are included only when the focal decision maker is human or GPT, respectively.
Model-by-model GPT composition is reported in SI Section 9, TableS25.
Leave-one-group summaries for F are reported in SI Section 7C, TableS22.
Fig 3.
Human transfer diagnostics.
A-B: Model-adjusted cooperation surfaces for the PD and SD stages in the two human PD+SD conditions.
The SD-stage estimates condition on the previous-round PD and SD cues that remained visible before SD as well as the same-round PD cue.
C: Primary human cue-use odds ratios are shown from the reduced-form transfer models, with PD-derived cues in orange and SD-derived cues in teal.
Values above one indicate that cooperation in the source cue predicts higher focal cooperation in the destination game.
D: Partner PD cooperation raised the partner's observed SD cooperation above the q = 1/3 Snowdrift best-response threshold.
E: Focal SD cooperation is shown after the full same-round PD outcome, where CC, CD, DC, and DD denote focal-partner PD outcomes, with cluster-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.
F: Partner-PD effects are shown separately among focal PD cooperators and focal PD defectors.
Anchored Latent-State Transfer Simulation Model.A: Visible prior history informs the PD-stage logit and a cross-fitted model of partner SD cooperation, qt .
The same-round partner-PD cue is excluded from qt and entered separately in the focal SD model.
B: Material-contrast loading and the remaining partner-PD coefficient are shown for humans and tested GPT configurations.
Because the cue is excluded from qt , this coefficient is predictive rather than a belief-adjusted social-value parameter.
C: Average cross-fitted partner-SD cooperation probability, qt , by round.
D: Observed and fitted focal SD cooperation after CC, CD, DC, and DD, with focal action listed first.
